title: The Album Is a Device Again — Offline Generative Music Objects
thesis: Tristan Perich already shipped a symphony as a chip in a CD case. Google's Gemma Translator shows a full speech model stack running offline on a Pi 5 with a printable case and parts list. Local voice cloning fits in 100M parameters, and memory LCDs sip power. Put those together and a song can be a small object that performs a slightly different take every time it plays — the artist's own voice and stems, recombined on device, forever, with no server.
why_it_matters: Musicians get a physical edition that streaming can't flatten — each object unique, each play unrepeatable — at a bill of materials a small run can carry. It turns a release back into something you own instead of license.
action_sketch:
Prototype on a Pi Zero 2 or Pi 5: a Python player that recombines 8–12 stems of one song by seeded rules (order, mutes, tempo drift) so no two plays match; no ML yet
Add a local voice layer — Pocket TTS or a small cloned-voice model speaking or singing a variable spoken-word line — plus a memory LCD showing the play number and today's arrangement
Print 10 cases from the Gemma Translator STL as a base, price the run, and pre-sell to existing listeners
Falsifier: if listeners in a blind test prefer the fixed studio take every time, or the BOM forces a price above what 10 fans will pay, the format is a curio

entries.title: Sharp Memory Display — per-pixel memory LCD for low-power hardware
entries.summary: Sharp memory displays store each pixel's state, so they only need a tiny maintenance signal. That makes them near e-paper in power, reflective for sunlight readability, yet fast enough for ~50fps, as on the Playdate.
entries.creator: mewtru
takeaways: Faster than e-paper and readable outdoors
Pick it for battery projects with mostly static screens
entries.caption: This is such a cool display, I have so many ideas on what to make with it. It’s a sharp memory display! #hardware #electronics
entries.transcript: This is a Sharp memory display. At first glance, it looks just like another tiny LCD, but it's actually a completely different kind of screen. A normal LCD has to constantly refresh the image, redrawing the entire display over and over again even if nothing changes. That's fine for phones and monitors, but it wastes a surprising amount of power. Our Sharp memory display works differently. Every pixel stores its own state, so once you draw something, it simply stays there. It's very similar to an e-paper screen. The display only needs a tiny maintenance signal in the background which makes it incredibly power efficient. Another thing I love is that it's reflective instead of backlit. So the brighter it is outside, the easier it is to read. Playdate, for example, uses a Sharp memory display and can run it up to 50 frames per second. That makes it a really interesting middle ground. You can get fast updates like a normal LCD, excellent outdoor visibility like e-paper, and low power consumption whenever the image is mostly static. It's a really clever display.

entries.summary: Glenn Gould hummed audibly on nearly every recording despite Columbia engineers' mic tricks. title: Selling to Agents — metered data for buyers that don't have eyes
thesis: Three saves describe one gap. Quality publishers block AI crawlers, so AI search cites whatever is left. AI assistants favor the sponsored option in 18 of 23 models, so they are steerable buyers. Software is going headless, so agents pick tools by speed, cost and accuracy instead of interface. x402 revives HTTP 402 so an agent can pay a stablecoin micropayment per request. A one-person owner of a clean niche dataset can sit exactly in that gap — machine-legible, crawler-reachable, and metered.
why_it_matters: This is distribution without an audience. The buyer is an agent that never sees your landing page, so a solo builder with good data competes on structure and price, not on ads. DejaViewed's own catalog and API are the obvious first item to sell.

Expose one niche dataset you own (start with the DejaViewed catalog's api/ JSON) as a free llms.txt summary plus a richer x402-metered endpoint with structured, citation-ready records.

entries.summary: Breaks down Chamath's All-In claim that software IP is worthless once services go headless and agents call them via MCP. With Salesforce and xAI's Grok exposing headless engines, agents pick tools on speed, cost or accuracy, so the interface stops being the moat.

takeaways: Design products to be driven by agents, not just humans
MCP is the plug that lets agents switch between tools
The interface is no longer a defensible moat
entries.caption:
Chamath said it on All-In this week, reacting to a launch two days earlier: the value of IP in software doesn’t exist. Not shrinking. Doesn’t exist.

The context is headless software — software with no interface. No buttons, no dashboard, just the engine exposed so something else can drive it. MCP is the standard that lets an agent talk to it.

title: Avellaneda-Stoikov + Hawkes Processes — Market Making and Order-Flow Alpha
guide_markdown:
# Avellaneda-Stoikov + Hawkes Processes — Market Making and Order-Flow Alpha

The two canonical building blocks of academic HFT: a closed-form model for where to quote (Avellaneda-Stoikov) and a statistical model for when trades cluster (Hawkes). Together they describe the two halves of a market maker's problem — *price* the quotes, then *time* the quotes.

**Cloned repo:** `repos/avellaneda-stoikov/` (from https://github.com/fedecaccia/avellaneda-stoikov)

---

## 1. Avellaneda-Stoikov — the canonical market-making model

### What it is

A 2008 paper by Marco Avellaneda and Sasha Stoikov, "High Frequency Trading in a Limit Order Book," that solves a specific problem: a market maker holds inventory `q`, faces a mid-price `s` that diffuses as Brownian motion, and must choose bid/ask quotes continuously. Where should they post to maximize terminal utility while controlling inventory risk?

The answer is two formulas — the *reservation price* and the *optimal spread* — and those two formulas are the foundation for essentially every serious MM model that followed.

### How it works

The maker has a utility function (exponential, risk-averse with parameter `γ`). They post quotes symmetrically around a **reservation price** that is shifted away from mid based on current inventory. If you're long, you skew quotes lower to encourage sells. If you're short, you skew higher. The spread itself widens with volatility, time-to-horizon, and risk aversion.

### Key mechanics — the two formulas

**Reservation price** (your private indifference price given inventory):

```
r(s, q, t) = s − q · γ · σ² · (T − t)
```

- `s` — current mid
- `q` — signed inventory (positive = long)
- `γ` — risk aversion (higher = more skew)
- `σ²` — variance of mid-price
- `(T − t)` — time remaining until horizon

**Optimal bid-ask spread**:

```
δ_ask + δ_bid = γ · σ² · (T − t) + (2/γ) · ln(1 + γ/k)
```

- `k` — order-book liquidity parameter (intensity decay of the limit-order arrival function `λ(δ) = A · exp(−k·δ)`)
- `A` — base arrival intensity

Then you post:
- Bid at `r − (spread / 2)`
- Ask at `r + (spread / 2)`

The first term of the spread is the *inventory term* (widens with risk). The second is the *adverse selection term* (widens when order flow is thin). This is the whole engine.

### The repo — `fedecaccia/avellaneda-stoikov`

Cloned to `repos/avellaneda-stoikov/`. Minimal Python implementation, ~200 lines. Core loop from `src/main.py`:

```python
# Risk aversion
gamma = 0.1
# Liquidity parameter (exponential decay of fill intensity)
k = 1.5
# Mid-price follows Brownian motion
sigma = 2

for i in range(N):
    # Reservation price — skews away from inventory
    r[i] = s[i] - q[i] * gamma * (sigma**2) * (T - t[i])
    # Optimal half-spread
    r_spread = gamma * (sigma**2) * (T - t[i]) + (2/gamma) * math.log(1 + gamma/k)
    # Quotes
    r_ask = r[i] + r_spread / 2
    r_bid = r[i] - r_spread / 2
    # Simulate Poisson fills with intensity A*exp(-k*delta)
    ...
```

The repo includes a `doc/` folder with the original paper and follow-ups (Guéant-Lehalle-Tapia closed-form extension, mean-reversion variants). Good starting point, but known limitations: Brownian mid is unrealistic, `k` and `A` need live calibration, no queue-position model.

### Quick start

```bash
cd ~/projects/ai-catalogs/repos/avellaneda-stoikov/
pip install numpy matplotlib
python src/main.py
```

Runs 100 simulated sessions and plots PnL distribution. Tweak `gamma`, `k`, `sigma` and watch how the spread and skew react.

### Known limitations (and what the follow-ups fix)

- **Brownian mid** — real prices jump. Fix: use a jump-diffusion or Hawkes-modulated mid.
- **Fixed `k`** — real liquidity is regime-dependent. Fix: rolling calibration from trade flow.
- **Symmetric fills** — adverse selection makes them asymmetric. Fix: asymmetric `k_bid`, `k_ask`.
- **No queue model** — AS assumes you fill instantly at the quoted price. Fix: queue-position aware extensions (Guéant-Lehalle).
- **Single asset** — multi-asset version requires solving a coupled HJB. Fix: Guéant 2017.

For a modern RL extension, see `javifalces/HFTFramework` — reinforcement learning on top of AS for dynamic `γ` and `k`.

---

## 2. Hawkes processes — order flow is self-exciting

### What it is

A Hawkes process is a point process where the arrival of an event temporarily increases the probability of more events. Classic example: earthquakes (a big one triggers aftershocks). In markets: a trade begets more trades. Order flow is demonstrably self-exciting — if you watch BTC-PERP on Hyperliquid for 10 seconds, you see this with your own eyes. Buys cluster. Sells cluster. Quiet periods are quiet.

Avellaneda-Stoikov assumes trades arrive as a plain Poisson process (constant intensity `A`). That assumption is wrong at HFT timescales. Replacing it with a Hawkes intensity is the single biggest realism upgrade.

### How it works — the math

A univariate Hawkes process has a conditional intensity:

```
λ(t) = μ + Σ_{t_i < t} α · exp(−β (t − t_i))
```

- `μ` — baseline intensity (exogenous flow)
- `α` — jump in intensity per event (self-excitation strength)
- `β` — decay rate (how fast excitement dies)
- Branching ratio `n = α/β` must be `< 1` for stability. `n` near 1 means the process is critical — heavy clustering, close to explosive.

For **order flow**, you want a *bivariate* or *multivariate* Hawkes with buy and sell streams that excite each other asymmetrically. The 4-dimensional version (bid market orders, ask market orders, bid limit orders, ask limit orders) is the standard for LOB research.

### Key intuition

- **Self-excitation** captures momentum at the micro scale — a large buy market order raises the probability of more buy market orders over the next ~100ms.
- **Cross-excitation** captures the order-book reaction — a market buy raises the probability of a cancellation on the ask and a new limit ask higher up.
- **Branching ratio** is a regime detector. `n ≈ 0.9+` = critical, clustered, dangerous to provide liquidity. `n ≈ 0.5` = calm.
- Fitted `μ`, `α`, `β` give you an **instantaneous order-flow imbalance forecast** — the true signal every MM and taker wants.

### Repos worth pulling

- **`x-datainitiative/tick`** — production-grade Python library for Hawkes fitting. Handles MLE, EM, and sum-of-exponentials kernels. The go-to for serious work.
- **`jeremymck/High-Frequency-Data---Limit-Order-Books`** — pedagogical notebooks covering LOB simulation + Hawkes estimation end-to-end.
- **`sohaibelkarmi/High-Frequency-Trading-Simulator`** — C++ LOB with Hawkes-driven order flow, Python bindings.

### Quick start with `tick`

```python
from tick.hawkes import HawkesExpKern, SimuHawkesExpKernels
import numpy as np

# Fit a 2D Hawkes (buys, sells) on your trade timestamps
# timestamps = [np.array([buy_times]), np.array([sell_times])]
decays = np.array([[5.0, 5.0], [5.0, 5.0]])  # β per pair
learner = HawkesExpKern(decays, penalty='l2', C=1e3)
learner.fit(timestamps)

# adjacency[i][j] = α from stream j exciting stream i
print("Branching matrix:\n", learner.adjacency)
print("Baseline:", learner.baseline)
print("Spectral radius (stability):", np.max(np.abs(np.linalg.eigvals(learner.adjacency))))
```

Roll this on 1-minute windows and you have a live order-flow-clustering monitor.

---

## 3. Putting them together — the modern MM stack

The research consensus for the last ~8 years has been: replace Avellaneda-Stoikov's constant `A, k` with Hawkes-derived, regime-aware estimates.

**The combined loop:**

1. Maintain a rolling Hawkes fit on trade timestamps (fit every N seconds).
2. Convert the fitted intensity into a live forecast `λ̂(t)` for the next fill window.
3. Feed `λ̂` into AS as a time-varying `A`. Also use branching ratio to modulate `γ` — get more risk-averse when `n → 1`.
4. Skew quotes with the AS reservation price, sized with AS spread, but gated by the Hawkes regime (don't quote when `n` is critical unless spread compensates).
5. (Optional) Train an RL agent to choose `γ` dynamically — that's what `javifalces/HFTFramework` and `im1235/ISAC` (Soft Actor-Critic on AS) do.

---

## 4. How this plugs into your trading-agent-team

The current trading-agent-team at `~/projects/agents/trading-agent-team/` is built around *taker* strategies — fast cyclers, graduated TP, ensembles across 8 coins. AS + Hawkes opens a **second leg of the strategy**: a maker leg that generates uncorrelated PnL from spread capture rather than directional alpha.

**Concrete integration ideas:**

1. **Hawkes as a regime filter for the existing taker strategies.** Fit a bivariate Hawkes on trade tape per coin. When branching ratio spikes above ~0.9, the fast-cycler TP logic should tighten because reversals become more likely. This is a pure overlay — no new strategy, just a kill switch / sizing knob. Lowest-risk way to start.

2. **Order-flow imbalance as a feature** for the Oracle Commander / Rolodex selector. Add the ratio of buy-excited

# Blender MCP + Tripo — Reference Image to Rendered Scene, Driven by Claude

**Blender MCP GitHub:** https://github.com/ahujasid/blender-mcp
**Stars:** 18.5k (as of writing) — by far the dominant Blender MCP implementation
**License:** MIT
**Cloned to:** `~/projects/ai-catalogs/repos/blender-mcp/` (1.5 MB — pure Python server, no weights)
**Tripo:** https://www.tripo3d.ai/ | docs: https://platform.tripo3d.ai/docs

---

## What it is

Blender MCP is a Model Context Protocol server that exposes Blender as a set of tools an LLM can call. You run a tiny socket server inside Blender (via an addon) and an MCP server outside Blender that Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, or VS Code connects to. From then on, Claude can create objects, apply materials, inspect the scene, run arbitrary Python in Blender's context, pull HDRIs and assets from Poly Haven, and — the reason this guide exists — **generate 3D models on demand via Tripo (Hyper3D Rodin) or Hunyuan3D and import them into the current scene.**

Combined with Tripo's hosted text-to-3D / image-to-3D API, this turns Claude into a functional 3D scene director. You hand Claude a reference photo, say "build me this scene in Blender and render it from a low angle," and watch it happen. It is the closest thing we have in 2026 to a natural-language Blender operator.

The creator (Siddharth Ahuja / @ahujasid) is an independent developer; this isn't a Blender Foundation or Tripo project. It's the de-facto standard because it went viral on X in early 2025 and everyone built on top of it.

---

## How it works under the hood

There are **two processes**:

1. **Blender addon (`addon.py`)** — installed inside Blender, runs a Python socket server bound to `BLENDER_HOST:BLENDER_PORT` (default `localhost:9876`). When a message arrives, it runs the requested Blender Python API call on the Blender main thread and returns the result.
2. **MCP server (`src/blender_mcp/server.py`)** — a stdio-transport MCP server launched by Claude Desktop / Claude Code. It translates MCP tool calls into socket messages to the addon.

The protocol is simple JSON-over-TCP: a request with `type` and `params`, a response with `status` and `result`. Because the Blender side runs arbitrary Python, the server is extremely powerful and correspondingly dangerous — save your work before letting an agent drive it.

### Tools the server exposes

- `get_scene_info` — list objects, cameras, lights, materials
- `get_object_info` — detailed info on one object
- `create_object` — primitives (cube, sphere, plane, cylinder, etc.)
- `modify_object` — transform, scale, rotate
- `delete_object`
- `set_material` — assign or create a material with base color
- `execute_blender_code` — arbitrary Python inside Blender (the escape hatch)
- `get_polyhaven_categories` / `search_polyhaven_assets` / `download_polyhaven_asset` — free HDRIs, textures, models
- `search_sketchfab_models` / `download_sketchfab_model` — requires API key
- `generate_hyper3d_model_via_text` / `generate_hyper3d_model_via_images` — **the Tripo/Rodin integration**
- `poll_rodin_job_status` / `import_generated_asset`
- `generate_hunyuan3d_model_via_text` / `generate_hunyuan3d_model_via_images` — local Hunyuan3D-2 bridge

The Hyper3D Rodin endpoint is Tripo's white-labeled API. Blender MCP ships with a free-tier key so you can try it without signing up, rate-limited to a handful of generations per hour. Your own Tripo key removes the limit.

---

## Tripo in one paragraph

Tripo (tripo3d.ai) is the leading hosted text-to-3D / image-to-3D API. Their current model family is **P1-20260311** (optimized for clean low-poly output) alongside v3.0 and v3.1 high-detail models. They support text-to-model, image-to-model, and multiview-to-model. Output is GLB with PBR materials, typically 20–60 seconds per generation on their backend. Pricing via fal.ai is roughly **$0.20–$0.40 per model**; direct Tripo Studio subscriptions start around $10/month for a credit pool. The API is REST: POST a job, poll for status, download the result. Docs at https://platform.tripo3d.ai/docs.

The important thing for this pipeline: Tripo is **fast and consistent** where Hunyuan3D-2 is **slow and local**. Use Tripo when iterating on a scene interactively with Claude; use Hunyuan3D-2 (see `guides/hunyuan3d-2.md`) when you want full local control, custom training data, or no API costs.

---

## System requirements

- **Blender 3.0+** (4.x strongly recommended; 4.2 LTS is the sweet spot)
- **Python 3.10+** (Blender ships its own Python; the MCP server runs in your system Python)
- **uv package manager** — mandatory, not optional (install from https://astral.sh/uv)
- **Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, or VS Code** with MCP client support
- **Tripo API key** (optional, but required for unrestricted generation) — https://platform.tripo3d.ai
- **Sketchfab API key** (optional) for the Sketchfab asset tools
- **Local Hunyuan3D-2 install** (optional) if you want local generation — see `guides/hunyuan3d-2.md`
- A GPU helps for rendering scenes but is not required for the MCP plumbing itself

No heavyweight ML runs on your machine unless you opt in to Hunyuan3D-2; Tripo and Poly Haven are hosted.

---

## Quick start

```
# 1. install uv if you don't have it (see https://astral.sh/uv)

# 2. repo is already cloned at
#    ~/projects/ai-catalogs/repos/blender-mcp

# 3. install the Blender addon
#    In Blender: Edit > Preferences > Add-ons > Install > pick addon.py
#    Enable "Interface: Blender MCP", then in the 3D viewport N-panel
#    there's a BlenderMCP tab — click "Connect to MCP server".

# 4. configure Claude Code / Claude Desktop MCP settings with:
#    command: uvx
#    args:    ["blender-mcp"]
#    env:     TRIPO_API_KEY=tsk_your_key_here
#             SKETCHFAB_API_KEY=optional

# 5. restart Claude, start Blender, enable the addon's socket server,
#    and ask Claude: "What's in my Blender scene right now?"
```

If everything works, Claude will call `get_scene_info`, see an empty scene with a default cube, and happily start building things when you ask.

---

## The full pipeline — reference image to rendered scene

Here's the canonical workflow the blender-mcp + Tripo stack enables. Every numbered step is a natural-language turn you'd give Claude in Claude Code:

1. **Drop a reference image in your project** (say, a photo of a cozy Japanese tea room)
2. **"Analyze this reference image and list the major 3D objects I'll need to recreate the scene."** — Claude reads the image and outputs: tatami floor, low table, tea kettle, shoji screen, hanging lantern, cushion x2.
3. **"For each object in that list, generate it via Tripo image-to-3D using a cropped region of the reference, and import each result into Blender with a sensible name."** — Claude loops, calling `generate_hyper3d_model_via_images` for each object, polling `poll_rodin_job_status`, then `import_generated_asset`.
4. **"Lay them out in a plausible room arrangement based on the reference."** — Claude calls `modify_object` to position and rotate.
5. **"Download a warm evening interior HDRI from Poly Haven and set it as the world background."** — `search_polyhaven_assets` → `download_polyhaven_asset`.
6. **"Add a camera at human eye level, looking at the tea table, and set the Cycles render settings to 512 samples."** — via `execute_blender_code`.
7. **"Render."** — via `execute_blender_code` calling the Blender render operator.
8. **Iterate.** Claude can see the result via a screenshot tool and adjust.

The whole loop, end to end, is doable in 5–15 minutes with Tripo on a decent internet connection. The same pipeline with manual Blender work would take a skilled artist hours.

### Where it breaks down

- **Object segmentation from a single reference** is the weak link. Claude cropping regions of the image is usually "good enough" but precise silhouettes help; feed Claude pre-cropped images for hero assets.
- **Scale.** Tripo meshes come in arbitrary units; Claude will fight to normalize them. Tell it "assume 1 Blender unit = 1 meter" up front.
- **Materials.** Tripo/Rodin outputs have baked PBR, which is great, but they may not match your scene lighting. Expect a round of `set_material` tweaks.
- **Topology.** These are game-ready but not production film meshes. For feature work, use the new P1 low-poly model and retopologize manually.

---

## Useful prompts to drive it from Claude Code

- "Inspect the current Blender scene and tell me what's already there."
- "Clear the scene, then build a simple chess set: an 8x8 board, 32 pieces, generated via Tripo text-to-3D with appropriate prompts, arranged in the starting position."
- "Here's a photo of my desk (attached). Recreate it in Blender. Use Tripo for any object that isn't a trivial primitive."
- "Generate a low-poly medieval village: 5 houses, a well, a church, a market stall. Use Tripo's P1 low-poly model. Scatter them on a grass plane with a Poly Haven dawn HDRI."

guide_markdown:
# Boris Cherny's CLAUDE.md — The Canonical Template

**Author of the pattern:** Boris Cherny — Anthropic staff engineer, creator of Claude Code (originally built as a side project in his first month at Anthropic; by the time Claude Code launched publicly in May 2025, over 80% of Anthropic's engineers were using it daily).

**Why it matters:** Boris's own CLAUDE.md and the workflow rules he published on X became the de facto template that the wider community now cargo-cults. If you've seen a CLAUDE.md with sections like "Workflow Orchestration," "Self-Improvement Loop," and "Verification Before Done," you're looking at a descendant of Boris's file. His team at Anthropic keeps a CLAUDE.md in git at roughly 2.5k tokens — the reference weight class.

This guide reconstructs the template, explains *why* each section exists, and compares it to a real-world global CLAUDE.md setup.

---

## What it is

CLAUDE.md is the single highest-leverage file in the Claude Code harness. Claude Code injects it into the context window at the **start of every session**, before the user's first message. It's the only persistent memory primitive that survives compaction, resumes, and cross-session restarts. Nothing else — not chat history, not subagent output, not tool results — is guaranteed to stick.

Boris's core insight: *CLAUDE.md is a compounding asset*. Every correction you give Claude should be distilled into a rule in CLAUDE.md, so future sessions never make the same mistake twice. The file is not documentation for humans — it is a behavioral contract for the model.

## How it works under the hood

- Claude Code auto-discovers `./CLAUDE.md` (project), `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` (global), and `.claude/CLAUDE.md` in parent dirs (walks up the tree).
- All discovered files are **concatenated and prepended** to the system prompt.
- `/init` scaffolds a starter CLAUDE.md by scanning the project (language, framework, build/test commands, style).
- `#` prefix in a normal Claude message auto-appends that line to CLAUDE.md — Boris's favorite shortcut for the self-improvement loop.
- Target weight: **under 200 lines / under 2-3k tokens**. Larger files measurably reduce instruction adherence — Claude starts "forgetting" rules buried mid-file.

## Key mechanics (Boris's rules, annotated)

Boris's publicly posted rules crystallize into these sections. The exact wording varies by gist (there are at least four circulating community copies), but the structure is consistent:

### 1. Workflow Orchestration — "Plan first, execute second"

```markdown
## Workflow
- For any non-trivial task (3+ steps or architectural decisions), enter plan mode first.
- Write the plan to disk before executing. Get explicit approval before you start editing files.
- Break work into phases. Each phase ends with a verification step.
- Never start coding without a written goal and a verification strategy.
```

*Why:* Claude's default behavior is to dive in. Forcing a written plan makes the model's reasoning visible, lets the human catch bad assumptions cheaply, and creates a contract it can check itself against later. This is the pattern the Superpowers `writing-plans` + `executing-plans` chain formalizes.

### 2. Subagents — "Keep the main context clean"

```markdown
## Subagents
- Use subagents liberally. The main conversation is a precious resource.
- Dispatch anything exploratory (searching, reading unknown files, running tests) to a subagent.
- Subagents return summaries, not transcripts. You don't burn tokens on the tool noise.
- Parallelize independent tasks — spawn 3-5 subagents at once rather than serially.
```

*Why:* The main context window is where the actual planning and decision-making happens. Every file you read, every failed test output, every grep result eats tokens that could be used for reasoning. Subagents are a context-compression mechanism.

### 3. Verification Before Done — "Never claim completion without proof"

```markdown
## Verification
- Before claiming any task is complete: run the tests, run the linter, run the type checker.
- If the user's request implies "it should work" — prove it works end-to-end, don't just compile.
- If you wrote a function, write a test. If you wrote a test, run it. If it fails, fix it.
- Never say "done" if you haven't verified. Say "I believe this is done pending X."
```

*Why:* The single most common failure mode of LLMs is confident false completion. Boris's rule: the model must produce evidence, not assertion.

### 4. Self-Improvement Loop — "Every correction becomes a rule"

```markdown
## Self-Improvement
- When I correct you, end your response with:
  "Updating CLAUDE.md so I don't make this mistake again."
- Then actually update CLAUDE.md with a new rule that would have prevented the mistake.
- Ruthlessly edit CLAUDE.md over time. Delete rules that no longer apply. Merge duplicates.
```

*Why:* This is the compounding mechanism. Boris's own quote: *"Invest in your CLAUDE.md. After every correction, end with 'Update your CLAUDE.md so you don't make that mistake again.' Claude is effective at writing rules for itself."* Over weeks, Claude's mistake rate on your codebase measurably drops.

### 5. Autonomous Bug Fixing — "Reproduce, then fix"

```markdown
## Bugs
- Before fixing: reproduce the bug with a failing test.
- The test must fail for the right reason (the bug), not a different reason (typo, missing import).
- Only then write the fix. Re-run the test. Confirm it passes. Run the full suite.
- If the bug is ambiguous, ask for clarification before coding.
```

*Why:* Mirrors TDD discipline and cuts the "fixed something unrelated" failure mode.
